generic_sampling_rules.int_primary_key: Sequential integers starting at 1, unique per table; never NULL.
generic_sampling_rules.int_foreign_key: Copy an existing parent primary-key value; never NULL (FK column is NOT NULL by PK role).
generic_sampling_rules.real_score: Uniform real in [8.5, 10.0] rounded to 3 decimals.
generic_sampling_rules.real_total: Uniform real in [50.0, 60.0] rounded to 3 decimals; no sum formula asserted.
generic_sampling_rules.real_age: Integer-valued real drawn from {15..40}, weighted toward 19-24.
generic_sampling_rules.real_height: Uniform real in [1.55, 2.05] rounded to 2 decimals.
generic_sampling_rules.text_name: Draw from a pool of realistic full names of 10-17 entries; allow accented/unaccented and case variants at ~15% share so 20-50% of rows share a name with another row.
generic_sampling_rules.text_place: Draw from a small pool of 6 city names; include 'Santo Domingo' and variant 'santo domingo'; allow case variants at ~10% share.
generic_sampling_rules.boundary_numeric: For each listed literal L, generate values L-step, L, L+step where step is the column's rounding step (0.001 scores, 0.01 measures, 1 for ages).
generic_sampling_rules.duplicates_for_distinct: Ensure 20-50% of rows share a value with another row on the targeted column via pool reuse.
generic_sampling_rules.ties_for_order: Ensure at least two rows share the same value on the ORDER column.
generic_sampling_rules.null_share: Schema DDL declares no NOT NULL constraints and observed null_rate is 0.0; therefore plant no NULLs in any non-PK column. All non-PK columns are sampled with non-NULL values only. This is stated explicitly to resolve the nullable-mismatch: the compact DB has zero NULLs and the generator matches that.
generic_sampling_rules.fresh_value_share: For text pools, ~80% of draws reuse a pool value (producing duplicates); ~20% are fresh on first appearance.

targets.rule: Generate people rows (n_people >= 8) and gymnast rows with n_gym <= n_people - 2; sample gymnast.Gymnast_ID without replacement from people.People_ID, guaranteeing at least 2 parent rows without children. No NULL FK (Gymnast_ID is PK).

Hometown: deterministically assign group sizes {0,1,2,3} across four distinct pool values (one pool value absent -> size 0, one appears once, one twice, one three times; remaining rows fill other pool values, at least one more pool value present twice elsewhere). Gymnast_ID: unique per person and PK; within a group of people by Hometown, COUNT(DISTINCT gymnast_id) can be 0 (no gymnast row), 1, 2, or 3 depending on how many of the group's people have gymnast rows; construction guarantees each of those group sizes exists for COUNT(DISTINCT) over the join. COUNT(*) over Hometown groups covers 0/1/2/3.

Hometown: 20-50% duplicate share via group-size construction (see aggregate_boundary). Name: 20-50% duplicate share via pool reuse; include at least 3 name values each appearing twice. Gymnast_ID: unique PK, no duplicates; distinct-count variation arises only via join multiplicity.

Hometown must include 'Santo Domingo' and the case variant 'santo domingo' in every instance (deterministic assignment, not probabilistic). Age: force at least one row each at ages 19, 20, 21, 22 so predicates age < 19/20/21/22 separate.
Intentionally unsatisfiable: People_ID is a unique PK so ORDER BY People_ID ASC has no ties at any rank. No construction required; no duplicate PKs may be introduced.

Apply after all other height assignment and after any null rule (no nulls planted anyway): with n_people >= 3, set heights[0] = heights[1] = max(heights) and ensure at least one other row has a strictly smaller height, so MAX(height) matches >= 2 rows and >= 2 distinct heights exist. Guard: only force when n_people >= 3.
Include at least one row each with Total_Points = 57.4, 57.5, 57.6 (the literal boundary 57.5 and one step either side); remaining rows drawn from [50.0, 60.0].

semantic_rules_and_formulas.formula: Hometown IN ('Santo Domingo','santo domingo','Bonao','Miami','Santiago de los Caballeros','La Romana','Los Alcarrizos')

semantic_rules_and_formulas.evidence: Observed Total_Points 57.374-58.061; range narrowed from [0,60] toward observed band. Sum formula dropped: row 4 (8.987+9.75+9.75+9.762+9.787+9.725=57.761 vs observed 57.649) contradicts it.

supporting_evidence.Total_Points_formula: Sum formula checked on rows 1 (58.061), 2 (57.924) and dropped on row 4 (57.761 vs 57.649); not asserted. Range rule uses observed min/max 57.374/58.061 with bound [50,60].
supporting_evidence.score_ranges: All six apparatus scores observed in [8.987, 9.787]; real_score uses [8.5, 10.0].
supporting_evidence.null_policy: DDL has no NOT NULL; observed null_rate 0.0 for every column; generator plants no NULLs and null_targets is empty. This explicitly resolves the engineer's nullable-mismatch by choosing option (b): restrict NULL planting to spec-marked columns (none).

generation_specification.uncertainty: Total_Points does not equal the sum of the six apparatus scores on all shown rows (row 4 mismatch), so no sum formula is asserted. Hometown group sizes {0,1,2,3} and Gymnast_ID distinct-counts are constructed deterministically given n_people=10, n_gym=7; if the size selector varies sizes, keep n_gym <= n_people - 2 and n_people >= 8 to preserve unmatched_join_rows and the size-3 Hometown group.

issues.evidence: Execution feedback lists every column of both tables as nullable: 'gymnast.Floor_Exercise_Points: generated rows: NULL 12 / 103', 'gymnast.Total_Points: NULL 12 / 103', 'people.Age: NULL 20 / 207', 'people.Name: NULL 20 / 207', etc. The schema DDL declares no NOT NULL constraints, so `_apply_null_rule` (instance.py) treats every non-PK column as nullable and plants ~10% NULLs. The specification's `null_targets` is empty and its `uncertainty` field states 'All columns are NOT NULL per statistics (null_rate 0.0), so null_targets is empty.' The program therefore contradicts the specification: it injects NULLs into columns the spec says are never NULL (scores, Total_Points, Age, Height, Name, Hometown).
issues.requested_revision: Reconcile the NULL policy. Either (a) the designer updates the specification to declare these columns nullable with a NULL share matching the compact DB (and the engineer keeps the current behavior), or (b) the engineer restricts `_apply_null_rule` to columns the specification actually marks nullable (currently none), so no NULLs are planted in score/measure/name/place columns. The two artifacts must agree; the current mismatch is a blocking inconsistency.

issues.evidence: spec.py defines `HOMETOWN_GROUP_SIZES = [0, 1, 2, 3]` and the specification's aggregate_boundary rule requires 'groups of size 0, 1, 2, 3 exist for COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT) over Hometown and Gymnast_ID'. However, `_people_rows` draws Hometown uniformly from `PLACE_POOL` (6 entries) plus boundary/variant draws; with n=10 there is no construction that guarantees a group of size 0 (a pool value absent from the instance), size 1, 2, and 3 simultaneously. `HOMETOWN_GROUP_SIZES` is defined but never referenced in instance.py. Similarly, `gymnast.Gymnast_ID` is sampled without replacement (`rng.sample(people_ids, n)`), so COUNT(DISTINCT gymnast_id) per group is always 1 — the aggregate boundary over Gymnast_ID is not constructed.
issues.requested_revision: Implement the aggregate_boundary construction explicitly: for Hometown, deterministically assign group sizes 0/1/2/3 across the pool (e.g. pick 4 pool values and assign counts 0,1,2,3, filling the rest arbitrarily); for Gymnast_ID, either allow duplicate FK values (so COUNT(DISTINCT) can exceed 1 within a group) or document that the boundary applies only to Hometown. Reference `HOMETOWN_GROUP_SIZES` in the sampler or remove it.

issues.evidence: The specification's `ties_for_order_limit` rule for `people.People_ID` says 'People_ID is unique; ties arise only if duplicates allowed — keep unique, no ties needed.' The program's `_people_rows` generates sequential unique IDs, consistent with this. However, the atomic-operations extraction lists `ties_for_order_limit` as a pattern with `tie_at_rank: any (no LIMIT)` and `direction: ASC`; the spec's resolution (no ties needed) is a design decision, not a program error. This is noted as consistent, not an issue — but the spec should state explicitly that the ORDER BY tie pattern is intentionally not constructed because the column is a unique PK, so the reviewer/engineer do not later 'fix' it by introducing duplicate PKs.
issues.requested_revision: Designer: add an explicit note in the specification that `ties_for_order_limit` on `people.People_ID` is intentionally unsatisfiable (unique PK) and no construction is required. No program change needed.

issues.evidence: `_height` in instance.py draws uniformly from [1.4, 2.1] and `_people_rows` forces `heights[0] = heights[1] = max(heights)`. This satisfies 'at least two rows share the maximum height value' and 'at least two distinct heights exist' only when n >= 2 and the two forced rows are not the only rows (otherwise all heights equal). With n=10 this is fine, but the rule is not robust to small n. Also, `_apply_null_rule` may set one of the two forced-max rows to NULL, breaking the 'two rows share the max' guarantee for non-NULL operands. The spec's `rows_with_different_values` rule targets `scalar:SELECT(MAX(people.height))` with 'qualifying_rows: >= 2 per group with different values'.
issues.requested_revision: Engineer: apply the max-height forcing after `_apply_null_rule` (or exclude the forced rows from NULL sampling), and guard the forcing with `n >= 3` so at least one other row remains to provide a distinct value. Alternatively, the designer clarifies that the rule is evaluated over non-NULL operands only and the current behavior is acceptable.

issues.evidence: The specification's `semantic_rules_and_formulas` includes `Total_Points BETWEEN 0 AND 60` and the `literal_pool` rule 'Include values around 57.5 (57.4, 57.5, 57.6)'. The program's `_total_points` draws from `TOTAL_POINTS_LITERALS` with 50% probability and otherwise uniform [0,60]. This is consistent. However, the specification's `supporting_evidence` notes 'All observed scores in [8.987, 9.787]' and the `real_score` rule uses [8.5, 10.0], while `Total_Points` uses [0, 60] — the two ranges are inconsistent in spirit (a sum of six scores in [8.5,10] would be in [51,60], not [0,60]). The spec explicitly drops the sum formula due to a row-4 mismatch, so this is a design choice, but the [0,60] range for Total_Points is much wider than the observed data and the score range would suggest.
issues.requested_revision: Designer: either narrow `TOTAL_RANGE` to a range consistent with the observed Total_Points values (e.g. [50, 60]) or document why [0,60] is retained despite the observed [57.6, 58.1] range. This is a specification-quality issue, not a blocking program error.

issues.evidence: `_gymnast_rows` samples `ids = rng.sample(people_ids, n)` when `len(people_ids) >= n`, which guarantees unique Gymnast_IDs but also means every gymnast row references a distinct person. The specification's `unmatched_join_rows` rule requires 'parent rows without children' — i.e., some people rows with no gymnast row. With n_people=10 and n_gym=7, at most 7 people are referenced, so at least 3 people are unmatched, satisfying the rule. However, the program does not explicitly construct this; it relies on the size difference. If `choose_table_sizes` varies sizes (e.g. people=9, gymnast=10), the rule could be violated. The execution feedback shows 20/20 valid instances, so in practice it holds, but the construction is not guaranteed.
issues.requested_revision: Engineer: explicitly ensure `n_gym < n_people` (or that at least one people ID is excluded from the gymnast FK pool) in `build_random_instance`, so the unmatched_join_rows rule is constructed rather than incidental. Alternatively, the designer documents that the rule is satisfied by the fixed table sizes (people=10, gymnast=7) and the size variation is bounded to preserve it.

issues.evidence: The specification's per_column_exceptions for aggregate_boundary claims that 'construction guarantees each of those group sizes exists for COUNT(DISTINCT) over the join' (0,1,2,3). However, the Hometown group-size construction in _hometown_assignment assigns sizes {0,1,2,3} to pool values, but _choose_gymnast_fk_subset then picks a size-3 group, a size-2 group, and a size-1 group by sampling from groups with len(pids) >= want. Because the size-3 Hometown group has exactly 3 people, taking 3 gymnast rows from it is possible, but the size-2 group may be the same group already consumed, and the 'size 1' plan may land on a group whose people were already used. The construction does not strictly guarantee COUNT(DISTINCT gymnast_id) values 0,1,2,3 across Hometown groups; it only attempts it. Execution feedback shows construction_pairs separated=10 of 60 eligible, with no per-group breakdown, so the aggregate_boundary separation is not demonstrated.
issues.requested_revision: Either (a) tighten _choose_gymnast_fk_subset to deterministically assign distinct Hometown groups to the 3/2/1 plans (e.g., pick three distinct groups with sizes >= 3, >= 2, >= 1 and sample disjointly), or (b) soften the specification's aggregate_boundary claim to 'attempted' rather than 'guaranteed'. This is a documentation/robustness issue, not a blocking error, since the pattern is a soft target and the program runs cleanly.

issues.evidence: The specification's generic_sampling_rules.real_height says 'Uniform real in [1.55, 2.05]', and spec.HEIGHT_RANGE = (1.55, 2.05). But the semantic_rules_and_formulas for people.Height says 'Height BETWEEN 1.4 AND 2.1'. These are consistent (the sampling range is a subset of the semantic bound), so no conflict. However, the rows_with_different_values rule requires 'heights[0] = heights[1] = max(heights) and ensure at least one other row has a strictly smaller height'. In _people_rows, the code sets the first two non-NULL heights to mx, but if the two chosen indices happen to be the only rows and all others are also mx (unlikely but possible with n=10 and uniform sampling), the 'strictly smaller' condition could fail. With n=10 and uniform [1.55,2.05], the probability that all 10 heights equal the max is effectively zero, so this is not a practical concern.

issues.evidence: The specification's literal_pool rule for gymnast.Total_Points requires 'at least one row each with Total_Points = 57.4, 57.5, 57.6'. issues.evidence: The specification's comparison_boundary for people.Age requires 'force at least one row each at ages 19, 20, 21, 22'. In _people_rows, the code does: if n >= len(spec.AGE_BOUNDARY): for k, v in enumerate(spec.AGE_BOUNDARY): ages[k] = v. This correctly forces the first four rows to 19,20,21,22. Good.

The specification's comparison_boundary for people.Hometown requires 'Santo Domingo' and 'santo domingo' in every instance. In _hometown_assignment, the code forces 'Santo Domingo' to pool[0] and ensures 'santo domingo' survives truncation. However, the truncation logic: pool = pool[:n_groups] where n_groups = max(4, min(len(pool), n)). With n=10 and len(pool)=7 (6 PLACE_POOL + 'santo domingo'), n_groups = min(7,10) = 7, so no truncation. Both values survive. Good.

The specification's duplicates_for_distinct for people.Name requires '20-50% duplicate share via pool reuse; include at least 3 name values each appearing twice'. In _name_assignment, target_dupes = min(3, n//2) = 3 for n=10, and vals = list(dupes) + list(dupes) gives 6 rows with 3 names each twice. The remaining 4 rows are filled from rest or dupes. This gives a duplicate share of at least 6/10 = 60%, which exceeds the 20-50% target. The specification says '20-50% duplicate share', but the construction produces >= 60% duplicate share (6 of 10 rows share a name with another row).
issues.requested_revision: Adjust _name_assignment to target 20-50% duplicate share (e.g., 2-5 rows sharing names) while still including at least 3 name values each appearing twice is contradictory: 3 names each twice = 6 rows, which is 60% of 10. The specification's two requirements (20-50% share AND >= 3 names each twice) are inconsistent for n=10. The designer should reconcile: either reduce to 2 names each twice (4/10 = 40%) or increase n_people. This is a specification inconsistency, not a program error per se, but the program follows the '>= 3 names twice' rule and violates the '20-50%' rule.

issues.evidence: The specification's duplicates_for_distinct for people.Name says '20-50% duplicate share' and 'include at least 3 name values each appearing twice'. For n_people=10, 3 names each twice = 6 rows = 60% duplicate share, which exceeds 50%. These two requirements are mutually inconsistent for the specified table size.
issues.requested_revision: Reconcile the specification: either (a) reduce NAME_DUPLICATE_GROUPS to 2 (4/10 = 40% share), or (b) increase n_people to at least 12 (6/12 = 50%), or (c) relax the 20-50% bound. The program currently implements the '>= 3 names twice' rule, producing 60% share.

The specification's rows_with_different_values for people.Height requires 'heights[0] = heights[1] = max(heights) and ensure at least one other row has a strictly smaller height'. With n=10 and uniform [1.55,2.05], the probability that all 10 heights equal the max is effectively zero, so a strictly smaller height will exist in practice.
